name: Oyster Grey
lede: Oyster Grey is a pale grey tinged with green and yellow, named for the mollusc, and again a name whose dictionary gloss runs brown.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
Paterson defines oyster grey as a brownish shade of grey, and files it among the greys [1]. For the plain word he gives oyster as a greyish white, first used as a color description in 1922, on the authority of Fowler's English Usage [1]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary, though, records oyster grey from 1894 [2]. The two dates need not conflict, since one is for the bare word and the other for the compound, but the library's record is the earlier one [1][2].

The swatch is greener than either description. The library calls it a "grayish greenish yellow", ISCC-NBS block 105 [2]. Its neighbors are the soft green-greys, [[sage-green]], [[olive]] and [[pearl-grey]], with plain [[grey]] as the family [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 554 carry this color over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed, more often than 79 per cent of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s: 45 of 1,674 paintings, 1.8 times the usual rate [3]. In 44 per cent of the 360 paintings where we measured its rank, it plays a light [3]. The earliest dated match is a painting by the Master of the Osservanza of about 1430, a floor not a first [3].
